DIESEL stress-tested as simultaneous wars target refineries

Global prices for diesel and other middle distillates remain close to record highs in real terms as simultaneous conflicts in the Middle East and Russia continue to disrupt refinery operations and export routes.

The wars have become increasingly interconnected, damaging some refineries, while leaving others unable to maintain normal output because they cannot source enough crude and other feedstocks, or export fuels they have produced.

Global refinery capacity has been effectively reduced by as much as 10%, according to some estimates, creating an acute shortage of fuels, rapid depletion of inventories, and intense upward pressure on prices ...

Improved profits at China’s state-owned oil majors are likely to help them deliver on Beijing’s demands for energy security.

Third-quarter earnings this week show PetroChina Co. and Sinopec reaping the rewards of higher oil prices caused by war in the Persian Gulf. The gains were mostly driven by upstream operations, although downstream businesses held up well despite China’s cratering demand for transport fuels. Offshore specialist Cnooc Ltd. reports later Friday.

Earlier this month, the government laid out key tasks for boosting energy security over the next decade. At a meeting with the National Energy Administration and other agencies, the three majors gave their plans for raising oil and gas reserves and output. #oott https://t.co/iSTcQHGHro

Canada’s shifting geopolitical alliances are neatly encapsulated by a 14-hour flight.

A direct link between Calgary and Abu Dhabi opened this week, connecting western Canada with the Persian Gulf nation for the first time. Saudi Arabia's 460,000 b/d Satorp refinery is operating at capacity, according to TotalEnergies' chief executive Patrick Pouyanne.
